"'''Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too'''" is the third and final episode of the fifth series of the anthology series ''[[Black Mirror]]''. The episode was written by series creator and showrunner [[Charlie Brooker]] and directed by [[Anne Sewitsky]]; it was released on [[Netflix]] on 5 June 2019, alongside "[[Striking Vipers]]" and "[[Smithereens (Black Mirror)|Smithereens]]".

It follows Ashley O ([[Miley Cyrus]]), a pop singer whose creativity is restricted by her controlling aunt, and Rachel ([[Angourie Rice]]) and Jack Goggins ([[Madison Davenport]]), teenage sisters who have recently lost their mother. The doll Ashley Too, owned by Rachel, is a clone of Ashley O's personality. Brooker based the episode on a sitcom script he had written years prior, about a [[punk rock|punk]] band who are hanged and return to life to find their manager profiting off their deaths. It was also informed by holographic performances featuring deceased artists.

The executive producers thought Cyrus would be perfect for the role, but were surprised when she agreed. Filming took place in late 2018, for five weeks, in [[Cape Town]], South Africa. Ashley O performs "[[On a Roll]]" and "Right Where I Belong" during the episode—these are adaptations of [[Nine Inch Nails]] songs. "On a Roll" was released by Cyrus, subsequently appearing on several national music charts as well as receiving a [[Guild of Music Supervisors Award]] nomination.

Critics found it to be more upbeat than most ''Black Mirror'' episodes. Ashley O's storyline was compared to Cyrus's own life, along with those of other figures in the music industry. Some reviewers analysed personality traits of Rachel and Jack as a reaction to their mother's death. Most critics found the episode lacking in structure, writing quality, exploration of themes and characterisation of Rachel, but Cyrus's acting received acclaim.

==Plot==
After the death of their mother, Rachel Goggins ([[Angourie Rice]]) and her [[bass guitar|bass]]-playing older sister Jack ([[Madison Davenport]]) live with their father Kevin ([[Marc Menchaca]]), who spends most of his time attempting to invent and promote [[Build a better mousetrap, and the world will beat a path to your door|mouse-control devices]]. Having recently moved, Rachel has no friends. For her fifteenth birthday, she receives Ashley Too (voiced by [[Miley Cyrus]]), an interactive [[Artificial intelligence|artificially intelligent]] robotic doll of her favourite [[pop music|pop]] star Ashley O (Miley Cyrus). Ashley Too encourages and tutors Rachel, who treats her as a friend, but their relationship annoys Jack. Rachel dances to Ashley O's song "[[On a Roll]]" at a school talent contest, but fumbles the end of her routine and leaves the stage embarrassed. Jack blames Ashley Too for Rachel's chagrin and hides the doll; Rachel accuses Jack of suppressing both Rachel's and her own creativity.

Meanwhile, the real Ashley O is unsatisfied with her life and wants to reinvent herself as a rock musician. When she writes broody music and does not take the medication given to subdue her, her controlling aunt and manager Catherine Ortiz (Susan Pourfar) laces her food with drugs to render her comatose. She and the unscrupulous Doctor Munk begin to extract commercially viable music material from Ashley's brainwaves. When the news reports that the coma was caused by a shellfish allergy, Jack apologetically returns Ashley Too to Rachel, who shows no interest.

Six months later, Ashley Too reactivates and begins to glitch out after seeing a news report on Ashley O's coma. Jack connects the doll to the diagnostic software Kevin uses for his humane [[mousetrap]] inventions and removes a limiter. Ashley Too reveals herself to be a duplicate of Ashley O's entire consciousness, and persuades Rachel and Jack to look for evidence of Catherine's crimes at her house. Jack inexpertly drives them there, then poses as a pest control technician while Rachel takes Ashley Too to where Ashley O lies comatose. The doll unplugs the life support to [[Assisted suicide|let her real self die]], but it transpires that the machine was actually perpetuating the coma and Ashley wakes up. Jack and Rachel subdue two staff members with Kevin's mouse stunner and a sedative syringe and flee the house with both Ashleys.

Ashley O directs the group to a venue where Catherine is debuting Ashley Eternal, a holographic replacement for Ashley O. Pursued by the police after Jack runs a red light, the group drive through the back entrance of the venue, dismaying Catherine and astonishing the crowd as Ashley O emerges on stage.

During the credits, Ashley O (now billed as "Ashley Fuckn O") performs the song "[[Head Like a Hole]]" in her pop rock style at a smaller venue, with Jack on bass. Rachel and Ashley Too watch while Kevin talks to the bartender about the venue's pest control. Two dissatisfied fans leave the concert as Ashley crowd-surfs.

A fifth series of ''Black Mirror'' was commissioned by Netflix in March 2018, three months after the release of series four.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/black-mirror-renewed-season-5-at-netflix-1090957|title='Black Mirror' Renewed for Season 5 at Netflix|work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|last=Strause|first=Jackie|date=5 March 2018|access-date=9 February 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234537/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/black-mirror-renewed-season-5-at-netflix-1090957|url-status=live}}</ref> Initially part of series five's production, the [[interactive film|interactive]] work ''[[Black Mirror: Bandersnatch]]'' increased in scope to the point where it was separated from the series and released as a standalone film; it premiered on 28 December 2018. Although previous series of the programme produced under Netflix contained six episodes, series five comprises three episodes, as the series creator [[Charlie Brooker]] viewed this as preferable to making viewers wait longer for the next series.<ref name="DS S5">{{cite news|url=https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a27568474/black-mirror-season-5-episodes/|title=Exclusive: Black Mirror's Charlie Brooker "[[Smithereens (Black Mirror)|Smithereens]]" and "Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too"—were released on Netflix simultaneously on 5 June 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.esquire.com/uk/culture/tv/a27475929/black-mirror-smithereens-striking-vipers-season-5-trailer-release-date-photos-cast-spoilers/|url-access=limited|title='Black Mirror' Season 5 ===Conception and writing===
[[File:Prince at Coachella 001.jpg|upright|thumb|alt=Prince|Holographic performances that used the image of dead musicians like [[Prince (musician)|Prince]] were an inspiration for the episode.]]
The episode was written by Brooker. It was based on a comedy sitcom script from years prior about a 1977 punk band whose members are hanged by a [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] minister and return to life to see their manager exploiting their deaths for profit. It also took inspiration from real life holographic performances of dead artists such as [[Prince (musician)|Prince]], [[Whitney Houston]], and [[Amy Winehouse]]; Brooker found the holograms "ghoulish" and noted that the subjects "often pass away in extremely tragic circumstances". He also considered AI as a means for creating a program which could imitate [[John Lennon]]'s songwriting or serve as a celebrity virtual assistant.<ref name="ew">{{cite magazine|url=https://ew.com/tv/2019/06/05/black-mirror-miley-cyrus-episode-interview/|title=''Black Mirror'' producers on that Miley Cyrus episode and a creepy pop star trend|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|last=Hibberd|first=James|date=5 June 2019|access-date=5 June 2019|archive-date=5 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190605090447/https://ew.com/tv/2019/06/05/black-mirror-miley-cyrus-episode-interview/|url-status=live}}</ref> Brooker said that the episode is not disparaging pop music, but criticising inauthenticity in music.<ref name="GQ"/> According to Brooker, an unused idea saw Catherine revealed as non-human, either with her face being removed to display the machinery behind it, or with her disappearing "in a puff of smoke". In the final episode, after her Ashley Eternal plan fails, she looks at the camera and breaks the [[fourth wall]].<ref name="ew"/>

===Casting===
[[File:Miley Cyrus Primavera19 -219 (48985546538) (cropped).jpg|left|thumb|alt=Miley Cyrus|Miley Cyrus was chosen to play the titular character Ashley O as well as voicing the character's robot counterpart, Ashley Too.]]
Brooker and Jones thought Miley Cyrus would be perfect for the part of Ashley O, but did not expect her to be interested, or that they would get a pop star for the role. However, she was a big fan of the programme, and within a couple of days of their reaching out, she accepted the offer.<ref name="Guardian interview"/><ref name="Wrap">{{cite web|url=https://www.thewrap.com/black-mirror-miley-cyrus-ashley-o-songs-head-like-a-hole-nine-inch-nails/|title='Black Mirror' Showrunners on Landing Miley Cyrus – and if They'll Release Ashley O's Songs (Video)|work=[[TheWrap]]|last=Maas|first=Jennifer|date=10 June 2019|access-date=15 May 2021|archive-date=15 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210515020345/https://www.thewrap.com/black-mirror-miley-cyrus-ashley-o-songs-head-like-a-hole-nine-inch-nails/|url-status=live}}</ref> She found the script's portrayal of the music industry realistic, in terms of its "overt exploitation of artists" and the way in which decisions are driven by performance metrics rather than creativity.<ref name="Guardian interview">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2019/jun/01/miley-cyrus-black-mirror-rachel-jack-ashley-too|title=Miley Cyrus: 'Black Mirror portrays the exploitation of artists'|work=[[The Guardian]]|last=Pelley|first=Rich|date=1 June 2019|access-date=15 May 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234824/https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2019/jun/01/miley-cyrus-black-mirror-rachel-jack-ashley-too|url-status=live}}</ref> Madison Davenport played Jack. She auditioned without knowing that the episode was part of ''Black Mirror'', and was only told about the scene where Jack distracts a bodyguard from investigating Ashley O's IV drip removal. She was sent the full script a few days prior to filming. Angourie Rice, who plays Rachel, auditioned later in the process and knew that it was for ''Black Mirror''.<ref name="Vulture"/>

The executive producer [[Annabel Jones]] said that the episode was about a musician trying to find her identity and "break out from the commercial machine". Jones said that Cyrus's personality matched how the episode gets more "heightened and sarcastic and satirical" as it progresses.<ref name="ew"/> She also said that Cyrus brought vulnerability to the role, despite her punk-like persona.<ref name="Wrap"/> Cyrus related to Ashley O's desire to explore other genres, something she did after becoming an adult. Cyrus said that her parents took an active role in her career and focused on getting a manager who would take care of her, in stark contrast to Ashley O's manager Catherine.<ref name="Variety interview"/> Cyrus contributed ideas about her character's clothing and appearance. She also spoke to Brooker about enjoying a recent performance to a mostly older audience who were not recording the experience on their phones. Some dialogue and ideas from this conversation inspired aspects of Catherine's presentation of Ashley Eternal.<ref name="ew"/>

===Filming and editing===
While the episode takes place in America, for financial reasons the filming went ahead in [[Cape Town]], [[South Africa]], taking place six days per week for five weeks.<ref name="Vulture"/><ref>{{cite news | url = https://inews.co.uk/culture/television/black-mirror-season-5-filming-locations-where-filmed-brazil-south-africa-kent-cape-town-sao-paulo/ | title = Where is Black Mirror season 5 filmed? Filming locations included Brazil, South Africa and Kent | first = Laura | last = Martin | date = 6 June 2019 | access-date = 6 June 2019 | work = [[i (newspaper)|i]] | archive-date = 7 June 2019 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190607150944/https://inews.co.uk/culture/television/black-mirror-season-5-filming-locations-where-filmed-brazil-south-africa-kent-cape-town-sao-paulo/ | url-status = live }}</ref> After Cyrus was spotted at the [[Victoria & Alfred Waterfront]] during filming in November 2018, rumours began that she would appear in the fifth series of ''Black Mirror''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nme.com/news/music/miley-cyrus-reportedly-filming-episode-black-mirror-2402406|title=Miley Cyrus is reportedly filming an episode of 'Black Mirror'|work=[[NME]]|last=Trendell|first=Andrew|date=14 November 2018|access-date=14 May 2021|archive-date=15 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210515020343/https://www.nme.com/news/music/miley-cyrus-reportedly-filming-episode-black-mirror-2402406|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.elle.com/culture/celebrities/a25090793/miley-cyrus-south-africa-black-mirror-episode-report/|title=Miley Cyrus Is Reportedly Shooting a 'Black Mirror' Episode|work=[[Elle (magazine)|Elle]]|last=Bailey|first=Alyssa|date=14 November 2018|access-date=14 May 2021|archive-date=15 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210515020428/https://www.elle.com/culture/celebrities/a25090793/miley-cyrus-south-africa-black-mirror-episode-report/|url-status=live}}</ref> Cyrus said that she was able to "get into Ashley" as she was isolated from friends and family. Problems in her personal life informed her emotions when portraying Ashley O's life breaking down. On the day that she filmed the scene where Ashley O wakes up from the coma, Cyrus had lost her home to a [[Woolsey Fire|California wildfire]]. She used the events to inform her acting, though she had to take some breaks during filming the scene.<ref name="Variety interview">{{cite web|url=https://variety.com/2020/tv/podcasts/miley-cyrus-black-mirror-britney-spears-sobriety-1234645223/|title=Listen: Miley Cyrus on 'Black Mirror,' Getting Sober and Her Love of Britney Spears|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|last=Malkin|first=Marc|date=23 June 2020|access-date=15 May 2021|archive-date=10 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210410030930/https://variety.com/2020/tv/podcasts/miley-cyrus-black-mirror-britney-spears-sobriety-1234645223/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The Ashley Too doll's movements were partly captured during the shoot, and partly [[computer-generated imagery]]. Two crew members controlled her movements—one for her head and arms, and the other for her wheels—and the doll spun around and spoke in real life. Some parts, however, required the actors to film with a [[green-screen]] stick, and the doll was added in during editing. The driving scenes were filmed on a [[sound stage]].<ref name="Vulture"/> The final scene was filmed in a Cape Town bar over the course of a few hours, on Cyrus's last day of shooting, with Davenport saying that it "felt like{{nbsp}}... a small punk venue". Davenport knew how to play the guitar, but learned the [[bass guitar]] over the course of a fortnight for her part in "Head Like a Hole". Cyrus and Davenport recorded the audio in a music studio.<ref name="Vulture">{{cite web|url=https://www.vulture.com/2019/06/black-mirror-madison-davenport-angourie-rice.html|title=''Black Mirror''{{'}}s Madison Davenport and Angourie Rice on Working With a 'Diva' Robot|work=[[Vulture (magazine)|Vulture]]|last=Ivie|first=Devon|date=11 June 2019|access-date=15 May 2021|archive-date=25 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210425235541/https://www.vulture.com/2019/06/black-mirror-madison-davenport-angourie-rice.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

During the writing process, Brooker contacted [[Trent Reznor]], the lead vocalist and songwriter for Nine Inch Nails, with a synopsis outline and an explanation that he wanted to adapt their music into pop songs.<ref name="GQ"/><ref name="Rolling Stone"/> Reznor—whose songwriting partner [[Atticus Ross]] produced the soundtrack to the series four episode "[[Crocodile (Black Mirror)|Crocodile]]"—was a fan of the show and approved. Brooker said that the humour arises from the fact that the pop versions are "insanely positive" and "full of empty affirmations". As an example, "On a Roll" changes the original lyrics "Bow down before the one you serve" to "I'm stoked on ambition and verve".<ref name="GQ"/> Reznor said that the songs were "wonderfully absurd" and "really funny" in context. He found it "strange to hear [his] music come through the blender and back".<ref name="Rolling Stone">{{cite magazine |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/trent-reznor-watchmen-pretty-hate-machine-interview-905456/ |title=Trent Reznor on 'Watchmen' Soundtrack, Nine Inch Nails' 'Pretty Hate Machine' Turning 30 |first=Kory |last=Grow |date=5 November 2019 |access-date=15 May 2021 |magazine=[[Rolling Stone]] |archive-date=16 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201116174642/https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/trent-reznor-watchmen-pretty-hate-machine-interview-905456/ |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Isobel Waller-Bridge]], sister of the actor and writer [[Phoebe Waller-Bridge]], received a credit for adapting the episode's music.<ref name="DoG"/>

==Analysis==
Adi Robertson of ''[[The Verge]]'' wrote that "Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too" is an "uncharacteristically upbeat story about subverting sinister tech toward good ends and combining a critique of celebrity fandom with a thought experiment about brain uploading".<ref name="Verge">{{cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/2019/6/7/18653290/black-mirror-review-season-5-rachel-jack-ashley-netflix-charlie-brooker-miley-cyrus|title=Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too is Black Mirror's stab at a feel-good teen comedy|work=[[The Verge]]|last=Robertson|first=Adi|date=7 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=25 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210525012111/https://www.theverge.com/2019/6/7/18653290/black-mirror-review-season-5-rachel-jack-ashley-netflix-charlie-brooker-miley-cyrus|url-status=live}}</ref> Tim Brinkhof of ''[[The New York Observer]]'' said that ''Black Mirror'' serves "to expose the lies and hypocrisies of society", in this case "conflict between the artistic integrity of the artist and the financial interest of their producers".<ref name="Observer">{{cite web|url=https://observer.com/2019/06/miley-cyrus-black-mirror-episode-charlie-brooker-criticized-for-wrong-reason/|title=Critics of Miley Cyrus' 'Black Mirror' Episode Can't See This Is Charlie Brooker at His Best|work=[[The New York Observer]]|last=Brinkhof|first=Tim|date=11 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=25 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225134222/https://observer.com/2019/06/miley-cyrus-black-mirror-episode-charlie-brooker-criticized-for-wrong-reason/|url-status=live}}</ref> Dan Stubbs of ''[[NME]]'' suggested that the title is a pun on ''[[Rita, Sue and Bob Too]]'' (1986), a film about two teenage girls who have a sexual relationship with a married man.<ref name="NME">{{cite web|url=https://www.nme.com/reviews/black-mirror-rachel-jack-ashley-review-season-5-episode-3-2505134|title=Black Mirror 'Rachel, Jack and Ashley, Too' review: a genius pop music caper that might better be called A Star Is Borg...|work=[[NME]]|last=Stubbs|first=Dan|date=5 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021}}</ref> Some critics noted a change in tone around halfway through the episode, with ''[[The Independent]]''{{'}}s Alexandra Pollard calling the latter half a "fun, high-concept heist film" and Stubbs describing it as "an adult take on the 1980s, kids' adventure caper, complete with gags [and] a goofy chase".<ref name="NME"/><ref name="Independent">{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/reviews/black-mirror-review-season-5-miley-cyrus-rachel-jack-and-ashley-too-charlie-brooker-a8943296.html|title=Black Mirror season 5: 'Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too' review – Miley Cyrus excels in an initially po-faced episode|work=[[The Independent]]|last=Pollard|first=Alexandra|date=5 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=11 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190611030356/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/reviews/black-mirror-review-season-5-miley-cyrus-rachel-jack-and-ashley-too-charlie-brooker-a8943296.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

"Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too" explores a number of themes that other ''Black Mirror'' episodes focus on, such as AI, storage of human memories, and drugs.<ref name="Vox"/> Stubbs said that it was "not so much science fiction as science fact", because technologies already exist to facilitate hologram performances and production of new music using an artist's voice and image without their consent.<ref name="NME"/> Robertson viewed it as "mostly allegorical", and employing technological tropes "to raise questions about human agency".<ref name="Verge"/> Writing in ''[[Vox (website)|Vox]]'', Alissa Wilkinson found that it asks: "What images are celebrities allowed to project? And what do their fans receive in return?"<ref name="Vox">{{cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/culture/2019/6/5/18650880/black-mirror-miley-cyrus-rachel-jack-ashley-recap-season-5-review|title=Black Mirror's Miley Cyrus episode rebels against positivity culture|work=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|last=Wilkinson|first=Alissa|date=5 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=17 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190617145719/https://www.vox.com/culture/2019/6/5/18650880/black-mirror-miley-cyrus-rachel-jack-ashley-recap-season-5-review|url-status=live}}</ref> Troy Patterson commented in ''[[The New Yorker]]'' that the episode criticises "people who tell kids to have faith in themselves because it suits their own cynical purposes", but nonetheless does "want kids to believe in themselves".<ref name="New Yorker">{{cite magazine|url=https://www.newyorker.com/culture/on-television/the-best-episode-of-the-new-black-mirror-is-a-princess-tale-starring-miley-cyrus|title=The Best Episode of the New "Black Mirror" Is a Princess Tale Starring Miley Cyrus|magazine=[[The New Yorker]]|last=Patterson|first=Troy|date=5 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=24 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210124042633/https://www.newyorker.com/culture/on-television/the-best-episode-of-the-new-black-mirror-is-a-princess-tale-starring-miley-cyrus|url-status=live}}</ref>

The episode makes small [[Easter egg (media)|Easter egg]] references to past works by Brooker. In Catherine's office, a cover of the magazine ''SugarApe'', from the 2005 sitcom ''[[Nathan Barley]]'', can be seen.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://inews.co.uk/culture/television/sugarape-nathan-barley-magazine-black-mirror-editor-294890|title=SugarApe: the awful, iconic Nathan Barley magazine returns in Black Mirror – and he's now the editor|work=[[i (newspaper)|i]]|last=Martin|first=Laura|date=6 June 2019|access-date=3 June 2021|archive-date=20 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120152825/https://inews.co.uk/culture/television/sugarape-nathan-barley-magazine-black-mirror-editor-294890|url-status=live}}</ref> Ashley O sings "[[Anyone Who Knows What Love Is (Will Understand)]]" by [[Irma Thomas]], a song which appeared in four previous ''Black Mirror'' episodes, first in "[[Fifteen Million Merits]]". A news programme references ''Sea of Tranquility'', a fictional franchise mentioned in "[[The National Anthem (Black Mirror)|The National Anthem]]" and "[[Nosedive (Black Mirror)|Nosedive]]", along with a number of events from other episodes. Rachel's high school is named after Colin Ritman, a ''Bandersnatch'' character, and Ashley O is treated at St. Juniper's hospital, which appears in "[[Black Museum (Black Mirror)|Black Museum]]", where it was in turn a reference to "[[San Junipero]]". Catherine can be seen using the Smithereen app from "Smithereens"; conversely, in "Smithereens", #AshleyOWembley is a trending topic.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vulture.com/article/black-mirror-season-5-easter-eggs.html|title=Every Hidden Easter Egg in ''Black Mirror'' Season 5|work=[[Vulture (magazine)|Vulture]]|last=Tallerico|first=Brian|date=7 June 2019|access-date=3 June 2021|archive-date=27 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210427182344/https://www.vulture.com/article/black-mirror-season-5-easter-eggs.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Characterisation===
[[File:Britney Spears, Roundhouse, London (Apple Music Festival 2016) (30072929931) (cropped).jpg|upright|thumb|alt=Britney Spears|The episode's storyline was compared to allegations that Britney Spears was forced to perform against her will during her legal conservatorship.]]
Many critics compared Cyrus's real life to the experiences of Ashley O. She is a singer-songwriter who garnered fame as the protagonist of the [[Disney Channel]] teen sitcom ''[[Hannah Montana]]'' (2006–2011). Similarly, Ashley O is a "peppy, cookie-cutter pop star", according to Kelly Lawler of ''[[USA Today]]''.<ref name="USAToday">{{cite web|url=https://eu.usatoday.com/story/life/tv/2019/06/05/black-mirror-season-5-recap-miley-cyrus-netflix/1331566001/|title=The Miley Cyrus 'Black Mirror' episode is Hannah Montana gone mad|work=[[USA Today]]|last=Lawler|first=Kelly|date=5 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=7 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201107233905/https://eu.usatoday.com/story/life/tv/2019/06/05/black-mirror-season-5-recap-miley-cyrus-netflix/1331566001/|url-status=live}}</ref> Brinkhof found the episode a "sharp critique on the ethics of stardom" that "eerily mirrors" Cyrus's "escape from her confining role" on ''Hannah Montana''. He said that "to what extent she has become the master of her own destiny or has remained caught up in the economic machinery remains uncertain".<ref name="Observer"/>

Earlier in 2019, Cyrus had mentioned "[[Free Britney movement|Free Britney]]" during a performance, in reference to allegations that [[Britney Spears]] was being subjected to abuse through her then-ongoing conservatorship.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://variety.com/2019/music/news/miley-cyrus-free-britney-spears-memphis-concert-1203205780/|title=Miley Cyrus Calls to 'Free Britney!' Spears at Memphis Concert|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|last=Willman|first=Chris|date=6 May 2019|access-date=1 June 2021|archive-date=29 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210329222610/https://variety.com/2019/music/news/miley-cyrus-free-britney-spears-memphis-concert-1203205780/|url-status=live}}</ref> Adam White of ''[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]'' noted the connection between the allegations and the narrative of "Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too".<ref name="Tele">{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-rachel-jack-ashley-review-miley-cyrus-shines-prescient/|title=Black Mirror: Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too, review: Miley Cyrus shines in a prescient, if vague, story with echoes of 'Free Britney'|work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]|url-access=subscription|last=White|first=Adam|date=5 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=5 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190605072953/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-rachel-jack-ashley-review-miley-cyrus-shines-prescient/|url-status=live}}</ref> The similarities drew renewed media interest in June 2021 after Spears delivered testimony in a court hearing alleging excessive abuse and control through her conservatorship, including being forcibly hospitalized and medicated against her will as punishment for refusing to perform.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Britney Spears testimony compared to 'haunting' Miley Cyrus Black Mirror episode|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/music/news/britney-spears-black-mirror-miley-cyrus-b1873296.html|website=[[The Independent]]|last=O'Connor|first=Roisin|date=26 June 2021|access-date=10 July 2021}}</ref> Robertson compared "Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too" to the same subject, as well as [[Kesha v. Dr. Luke|legal disputes]] between the singer [[Kesha]] and her former producer [[Dr. Luke]].<ref name="Verge"/> According to Stubbs, Catherine "views a vulnerable dependant as a product" and is in this way comparable to [[Murry Wilson]] and [[Joe Jackson (manager)|Joe Jackson]].<ref name="NME"/>

Critics commented on how the death of Rachel and Jack's mother affected the children. David Sims of ''[[The Atlantic]]'' said that both children experience depression, "with Rachel retreating into herself{{nbsp}}... while Jack lashes out against the world".<ref name="Atlantic">{{cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2019/06/black-mirror-season-5-rachel-jack-and-ashley-too-review/590740/|title=Black Mirror: 'Rachel, Jack, and Ashley Too' Is a Fascinating Jumble|work=[[The Atlantic]]|url-access=limited|last=Sims|first=David|date=5 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=5 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190605161302/https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2019/06/black-mirror-season-5-rachel-jack-and-ashley-too-review/590740/|url-status=live}}</ref> Robertson thought the start of the episode "offers a fittingly melancholic portrait of someone using an imaginary relationship to handle loss and anxiety".<ref name="Verge"/> Patterson wrote: "Where Ashley O is a kind of Pinocchio dreaming of becoming a real girl, Rachel and Jack Goggins are two sisters awaiting their discovery as princesses". He said the lack of a maternal figure "abets its qualities as a fairy tale".<ref name="New Yorker"/> In order to "cope with lonely teenage hell", Robertson said that Rachel does "idol worship" of Ashley O. This connection draws on "the increasingly reciprocal relationship between celebrities and their fans."<ref name="Verge"/> The Ashley Too doll was compared variously to the robotic toy [[Furby]], the virtual assistant [[Amazon Alexa]] and the fictional virtual assistant Samantha from ''[[Her (2013 film)|Her]]'' (2013).<ref name="DoG"/><ref name="Vox"/> In contrast with an episode of ''[[The Simpsons]]'' on a similar topic, "[[Lisa vs. Malibu Stacy]]" (1994), Rachel is not critical of her doll.<ref name="Paste"/>

Wilkinson compared Rachel to Kayla, the protagonist of the comedy-drama film ''[[Eighth Grade (film)|Eighth Grade]]'' (2018). Kayla is a young girl who films little-viewed [[YouTube]] videos about positivity. Wilkinson said that the documentary ''[[Jawline (film)|Jawline]]'' (2019) demonstrates "an eventual cost to the producers of that kind of relentless optimism, especially when the teenage content creators can't keep it up because things at home actually aren't all that great": this is similar to Ashley O's unhappy private life. Wilkinson wrote that "Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too" shows "repercussions for the audience too", as a person views themselves as a failure for being unhappy. She asks: "is it the celebrity performance packaging industry itself that's at fault? Or is it the creators? Or the fans?"<ref name="Vox"/> On the same note, Zack Handlen of ''[[The A.V. Club]]'' commented that "'empowerment' has become a brand, with generic messages of confidence and believe-in-yourself churned out for an audience desperate to hear any assurance that there might be some way out of their misery".<ref name="AVClub">{{cite web|url=https://www.avclub.com/black-mirror-reminds-us-that-sometimes-unhappy-people-s-1835276280|title=Black Mirror reminds us that sometimes unhappy people sing happy songs|work=[[The A.V. Club]]|last=Handlen|first=Zack|date=5 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021}}</ref>

==Reception==
The episode holds a 51% rating on [[Rotten Tomatoes]], based on 41 critics, indicating mixed reviews. Its critics' consensus summarises that it "struggles to sew its many concepts together", and the most major strength is Cyrus's "wholly committed and compelling performance".<ref>{{cite web |title=Black Mirror – Season 5, Episode 3 |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s05/e03 |publisher=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] |access-date=1 June 2021 |archive-date=25 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190725232147/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s05/e03 |url-status=live }}</ref> It received ratings of three out of five stars in ''The Telegraph'' and ''The Independent'', and two stars from the [[BBC]].<ref name="Independent"/><ref name="Tele"/><ref name="BBC"/> It was rated 5.5 out of 10 in ''Paste'' and graded C+ in ''The A.V. Club''.<ref name="Paste"/><ref name="AVClub"/> The critics Brinkhof, Patterson and Sims thought it was the best episode of series five, while ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]''{{'}}s Jim Vorel and ''[[The Guardian]]''{{'}}s Stuart Heritage found it the worst, with Heritage adding that it was one of the worst episodes of ''Black Mirror'' overall.<ref name="Observer"/><ref name="New Yorker"/><ref name="Atlantic"/><ref name="Paste">{{cite web|url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/tv/black-mirror/black-mirror-season-5-episode-3-review/|title=Miley Cyrus Flounders in Black Mirror's Self-Parodying "Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too"|work=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]|last=Vorel|first=Jim|date=5 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=25 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210425221916/https://www.pastemagazine.com/tv/black-mirror/black-mirror-season-5-episode-3-review/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Guardian">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2019/jun/07/black-mirror-miley-cyrus-rachel-jack-ashley-too|title=Out of tune: why Miley Cyrus' Black Mirror episode hits the wrong note|work=[[The Guardian]]|last=Heritage|first=Stuart|date=7 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=3 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210503144813/https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2019/jun/07/black-mirror-miley-cyrus-rachel-jack-ashley-too|url-status=live}}</ref>

Hugh Montgomery, writing in the BBC, criticised the episode as ''Black Mirror'' "at its most crudely parabolic".<ref name="BBC">{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20190603-black-mirror-series-5-review|title=Black Mirror series 5 review|publisher=[[BBC]]|last=Montgomery|first=Hugh|date=5 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=9 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209234614/https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20190603-black-mirror-series-5-review|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[The Hollywood Reporter]]''{{'}}s Tim Goodman characterised it as an unintentional "Disney movie spoof" due to its "ridiculous plot and obvious writing".<ref name="THR">{{cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-reviews/black-mirror-review-1215653/|title='Black Mirror' Season 5: TV Review|work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|last=Goodman|first=Tim|date=4 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=16 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210516195108/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-reviews/black-mirror-review-1215653/|url-status=live}}</ref> Robertson and Daniel D'Addario of ''[[Variety (website)|Variety]]'' believed it was worse than most ''Black Mirror'' episodes, with Robertson finding it a "corny, scattershot installment of a show that's usually revered for its sharp cynicism", and D'Addario calling it "the most majestically wrongheaded" episode of ''Black Mirror'' and of "prestige television" in the latest year.<ref name="Verge"/><ref name="Variety">{{cite web|url=https://variety.com/2019/tv/columns/miley-cyrus-black-mirror-rachel-jack-and-ashley-1203232651/|title=The Unfulfilled Potential of Miley Cyrus' 'Black Mirror' Episode (Column)|work=[[Variety (website)|Variety]]|last=D'Addario|first=Daniel|date=4 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=2 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210302140939/https://variety.com/2019/tv/columns/miley-cyrus-black-mirror-rachel-jack-and-ashley-1203232651/|url-status=live}}</ref> However, Sims found it an "intermittently fascinating bit of pop-music melodrama", albeit "bizarre", and Heritage approved that it was not "pointlessly bleak for the sake of it".<ref name="Atlantic"/>

Some critics said the episode contained interesting ideas, but that these were insufficiently explored. Brinkhof pointed to "[[Be Right Back]]" and "[[White Christmas (Black Mirror)|White Christmas]]" as past episodes that examined themes of cloning and AI more deeply, and wrote that fans "lamented" the episode "for its untapped potential".<ref name="Observer"/> D'Addario said that the episode "has about fifteen potentially fruitful topics on its mind" but fails to find a good continuation from the premise. An example interesting topic is "women in music presenting a show of empowerment while being financially and creatively under someone else's control". D'Addario pointed to the "fundamental unseriousness of tone" as a reason the episode does not properly explore its themes.<ref name="Variety"/> White found "fascinating ideas sketched here and there", but a reliance on "vaguely banal statements on the vapidity of pop and the lack of care afforded to some of its most profitable stars".<ref name="Tele"/> Dissenting, Sims argued that "Brooker does a solid job interpolating" between "three big ideas", where "no single theme gets to dominate or develop fully".<ref name="Atlantic"/>

Patterson wrote that the show was "sharpest in its revisionist considerations of genre", and approved that the episode "tinkers with the tropes of tween tales and talks back to the genre in its own voice and on its own terms".<ref name="New Yorker"/> Sims thought the Ashley Too doll's consciousness was the "most compelling" idea, though it "arrives late in a muddled tale" as a "third-act plot twist", and Robertson saw "huge untapped potential" in having Rachel choose between the real Ashley O and the "perfect, locked-down" Ashley Too, or exploring the identity conflict between Ashley O and Ashley Too.<ref name="Verge"/><ref name="Atlantic"/> Handlen asks why Ashley O's consciousness would be uploaded into the doll when it does not "do anything that much more complicated than empty pleasantries and soundbites".<ref name="AVClub"/> In contrast, ''[[Den of Geek]]''{{'}}s Rob Leane found it "brilliantly designed" and funny.<ref name="DoG">{{cite web|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-5-rachel-jack-and-ashley-too-review-a-tour-de-force-from-miley-cyrus/|title=Black Mirror season 5: Rachel, Jack And Ashley Too review – a tour-de-force from Miley Cyrus|work=[[Den of Geek]]|last=Leane|first=Rob|date=5 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=8 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201108000303/https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-5-rachel-jack-and-ashley-too-review-a-tour-de-force-from-miley-cyrus/|url-status=live}}</ref> Chelsea Steiner of ''[[The Mary Sue]]'' said that the episode "offers nothing new or nuanced" in its "poking fun at vapid pop music", a topic well-explored by other works.<ref name="Mary">{{cite web|url=https://www.themarysue.com/black-mirror-rachel-jack-and-ashley-too/|title=''Black Mirror''{{'}}s "Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too" Embodies the Shallow Feminism It Attempts to Skewer|work=[[The Mary Sue]]|last=Steiner|first=Chelsea|date=12 June 2019|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-date=22 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201022164039/https://www.themarysue.com/black-mirror-rachel-jack-and-ashley-too/|url-status=live}}</ref> Heritage listed ''[[A Star Is Born (2018 film)|A Star Is Born]]'' (2018), ''[[Vox Lux]]'' (2018) and ''[[Yesterday (2019 film)|Yesterday]]'' as recent works that also addressed how "young creatives are at the mercy of their morally bankrupt handlers".<ref name="Guardian"/>

Reviewers were largely disappointed by the writing and structure. Pollard summarised that: "Plot points are picked up and dropped; narrative arcs lead to nowhere; unnecessary characters abound".<ref name="Independent"/> A change in tone midway through was widely commented on, with Handlen writing that "we don't actually get to the plot till about the forty minute mark". According to Handlen, it starts as a "low-key family drama" and becomes a "kid's adventure film".<ref name="AVClub"/> Robertson found that after "a promising start", the storyline "becomes simultaneously overstuffed and underveloped", omitting "the intimate details that make its early scenes so compelling".<ref name="Verge"/> Montgomery analysed the latter half as a "hokey-teen-sci-fi-adventure" that is "increasingly ludicrous and puerile" and Robertson said that episode was "at its blandest during some deeply unnecessary action sequences".<ref name="Verge"/><ref name="BBC"/> Vorel criticised "clear-cut heroes and villains" with "paper-thin degrees of depth", and Sims believed the villains to be "particularly overwrought" as the episode does not explore their motivations.<ref name="Atlantic"/><ref name="Paste"/> However, Leane praised that "an array of toe-tapping tunes{{nbsp}}... really assist the episode in making this pop icon feel real".<ref name="DoG"/>

The ending received mixed commentary, as did some individual scenes. It was described as "gratifying" by Patterson, "a really triumphant payoff" by Leane and a "fantastic surprise" that subverted "the trademark nihilism" by White.<ref name="DoG"/><ref name="New Yorker"/><ref name="Tele"/> However, Sims accused the episode of being "more interested in providing a neat ending than in delving into the deep questions it stirs up", and Brinkhof reported that some fans "accuse its feel-good ending of being a symptom of the infamously bleak show losing its uncompromisingly sinister edge".<ref name="Atlantic"/> Leane reviewed that the mouse trap concept "feels like filler", though its payoff was "quite funny".<ref name="DoG"/> Sims praised one particular scene, wherein Ashley O's comatose musical ideas are turned into pop music, as "a classic piece of grim ''Black Mirror'' humor".<ref name="Atlantic"/>

Cyrus received acclaim for her portrayal of Ashley O and Ashley Too. Lawler said that "Cyrus is essentially playing herself{{nbsp}}... and she does it well".<ref name="USAToday"/> Goodman said she was "one of the few actresses and singers who could even make this work".<ref name="THR"/> Pollard analysed that Cyrus was most impressive at playing the "two extremes" of her character's emotions: "desperate and broken" on one end and "uninhibited and defiant" on the other.<ref name="Independent"/> Montgomery found her early "subdued, spectral performance" as Ashley O to be the best part of the episode.<ref name="BBC"/> Leane and Sims both enjoyed her voice acting as Ashley Too, with Leane calling it a "tour-de-force performance" and Sims finding her "especially charming" in the role.<ref name="DoG"/><ref name="Atlantic"/> However, Robertson preferred her as Ashley O, writing that Ashley Too is a "generic robot sidekick".<ref name="Verge"/> In contrast, Vorel criticised the characterisation of both versions, saying that the idea "could have come straight from Cyrus' own marketing team, in a meta-attempt to prove that Miley Cryus The Performer is a being of depth and nuance".<ref name="Paste"/> Heritage saw writing problems in Ashley O's later dialogue, saying that she "stops sounding like Miley Cyrus and starts sounding like a 48-year-old man trying to sound like Miley Cyrus".<ref name="Guardian"/>

Other characters received less praise. Vorel found Rachel to be so "hopelessly naive" that the viewer "can't reasonably be expected to identify with or even empathize with her".<ref name="Paste"/> Handlen crticised that Rachel "is basically forgotten once the story kicks in", while Vorel said that Jack "rarely amounts to more than a sounding board for Rachel's insecurities".<ref name="Paste"/><ref name="AVClub"/> Steiner wrote that the episode fails to understand teenage girls and criticised an overall lack of "an authentic voice for any of the leads", suggesting that having a woman writer may have averted this problem.<ref name="Mary"/> Leane experienced a "minor letdown" in the lack of "emotional punch" in scenes showing Rachel and Jack with their father. However, he praised that "the core characters all get their chance to shine in a musical number".<ref name="DoG"/>

"Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too" ranked as follows on critics' lists of the 23 instalments of ''Black Mirror'', from best to worst:
{{col-begin}}
{{col-2}}
* 9th – Matt Miller, ''[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.esquire.com/entertainment/tv/a49919/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/|url-access=limited|title=Every Episode of Black Mirror, Ranked|date=5 June 2019|first1=Corey|last1=Atad|first2=Matt|last2=Miller|website=[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115155037/https://www.esquire.com/entertainment/tv/a49919/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=2 June 2021}}</ref>
* 14th – Ed Power, ''The Telegraph''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-best-episodes-worst-ranked/|title=Black Mirror: best and worst episodes ranked, from Striking Vipers to San Junipero|date=5 June 2020|first=Ed|last=Power|website=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]|url-access=subscription|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115155347/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-best-episodes-worst-ranked/|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=2 June 2021}}</ref>
* 15th – Aubrey Page, ''[[Collider (website)|Collider]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://collider.com/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/|title=Every 'Black Mirror' Episode Ranked From Worst to Best|date=10 October 2020|first=Aubrey|last=Page|work=[[Collider (website)|Collider]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115154650/https://collider.com/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=2 June 2021}}</ref>
* 17th – [[James Hibberd (writer)|James Hibberd]], ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]''<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://ew.com/gallery/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/?slide=6274289#6274289|title=Every Black Mirror episode ranked|date=9 April 2020|author=[[James Hibberd (writer)|Hibberd, James]]|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|access-date=2 June 2021}}</ref>
{{col-2}}
* 18th – Charles Bramesco, ''[[Vulture (magazine)|Vulture]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vulture.com/2016/10/every-black-mirror-episode-from-worst-to-best.html|url-access=limited|title=Every Black Mirror Episode, Ranked|date=5 June 2019|first=Charles|last=Bramesco|website=[[Vulture (website)|Vulture]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115160525/https://www.vulture.com/2016/10/every-black-mirror-episode-from-worst-to-best.html|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=2 June 2021}}</ref>
* 18th – Tim Molloy, ''[[TheWrap]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thewrap.com/striking-vipers-black-mirror-episodes-ranked-san-junipero-ashley-san-junipero/|title='Striking Vipers' to 'San Junipero': Every 'Black Mirror' Episode Ranked, From Good to Mind-Blowing (Photos)|date=8 June 2019|first=Tim|last=Molloy|website=[[TheWrap]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201113105133/https://www.thewrap.com/striking-vipers-black-mirror-episodes-ranked-san-junipero-ashley-san-junipero/|archive-date=13 November 2020|url-status=live|access-date=2 June 2021}}</ref>
* 22nd – Morgan Jeffery and Rosie Fletcher, ''[[Digital Spy]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a780434/black-mirror-episodes-ranked-charlie-brooker/|title=Ranking all 23 episodes of Charlie Brooker's chilling Black Mirror|date=13 June 2019|first1=Morgan|last1=Jeffery|first2=Rosie|last2=Fletcher|work=[[Digital Spy]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111225039/https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a780434/black-mirror-episodes-ranked-charlie-brooker/|archive-date=11 November 2020|url-status=live|access-date=2 June 2021}}</ref>
* 23rd – Travis Clark, ''[[Business Insider]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/every-black-mirror-episode-on-netflix-ranked-from-worst-to-best-2018-5|title=All 23 episodes of Netflix's 'Black Mirror,' ranked from worst to best|date=10 June 2019|first=Travis|last=Clark|website=[[Business Insider]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180911115114/https://www.businessinsider.com/every-black-mirror-episode-on-netflix-ranked-from-worst-to-best-2018-5|archive-date=11 September 2018|url-status=live|access-date=2 June 2021}}</ref>
{{col-end}}

''[[IndieWire]]'' authors ranked the 22 ''Black Mirror'' instalments excluding ''Bandersnatch'' by quality, giving "Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too" a position of 16th.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.indiewire.com/2017/11/best-black-mirror-episodes-worst-netflix-ranked-1201897973/|title=Every 'Black Mirror' Episode Ranked, From Worst to Best|last1=Greene|first1=Steve|last2=Nguyen|first2=Hanh|last3=Miller|first3=Liz Shannon|work=[[IndieWire]]|date=24 November 2017|access-date=2 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201203010214/https://www.indiewire.com/2017/11/best-black-mirror-episodes-worst-netflix-ranked-1201897973/|archive-date=3 December 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> Instead of by quality, Proma Khosla of ''[[Mashable]]'' ranked the episodes by tone, concluding that "Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too" was the fourth-least pessimistic episode of the show.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mashable.com/2018/01/05/black-mirror-pessimism-ranking-dread/|title=Every 'Black Mirror' episode ever, ranked by overall dread|date=5 January 2018|first=Proma|last=Khosla|work=[[Mashable]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115161226/https://mashable.com/2018/01/05/black-mirror-pessimism-ranking-dread/|archive-date=15 January 2021|url-status=live|access-date=2 June 2021}}</ref>

===Awards===
{{See also|List of awards and nominations received by Black Mirror}}
In 2020, "On a Roll" received a nomination for a [[Guild of Music Supervisors Award]] in the category Song Written and/or Recorded for Television, with Trent Reznor as the songwriter, Miley Cyrus as the artist and Amelia Hartley as music supervisor.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lists/guild-music-supervisors-awards-2020-winners-list-full-1275905/television-musical-or-comedy-2/|title=Guild of Music Supervisors Awards: 'Once Upon a Time,' 'Queen & Slim' Among Winners|work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|last1=Nordyke|first1=Kimberly|last2=Howard|first2=Annie|date=7 February 2020|access-date=14 May 2021|archive-date=14 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210514152919/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lists/guild-music-supervisors-awards-2020-winners-list-full-1275905/television-musical-or-comedy-2/|url-status=live}}</ref>
